//: STACK JUSTIFICATION (package.json can't hold a real comment, so it lives here):
React 18 + Vite + TypeScript, nothing else load-bearing.
- Vite over CRA: CRA is unmaintained and its dev-server rebuild time (webpack, full reload) doesn't fit a
2-day single-dev build with a live-polling view under active iteration. Vite's esbuild dev server and
native ESM HMR make the poll-driven UI genuinely fast to iterate on.
- React over Vanilla TS: this app is state-machine-shaped (7 stage nodes each with independent
status/attempt/duration, three concurrent poll-driven views, gate approval flows with optimistic
updates). React's reconciliation is exactly the right tool for 'render N nodes whose state changes
independently and rapidly on a poll tick' -- hand-rolling that in vanilla TS is solved-problem
reinvention for zero benefit at this scope.
- React over Next.js: Next's value is SSR/SSG/file routing/API routes. This is a local-only SPA against
one existing Spring Boot API with three views and no SEO surface -- none of Next's machinery earns its
keep here, and it would add a build/runtime model the assessment doesn't need.
- No UI library (MUI/Ant/Chakra/shadcn/Radix): the brief explicitly wants something that doesn't read as
a template, and every one of these libraries has a visual signature a senior reviewer recognizes on
sight. Hand-written components also mean every spacing/color/motion value traces back to tokens.css,
not a library's internal defaults fighting the override layer.
- No Tailwind: utility-class soup in JSX obscures the actual design decisions and makes 'why is this
16px and not 12px' unanswerable at a glance. Plain CSS modules-per-component, all values sourced from
tokens.css custom properties, keep every decision inspectable and intentional.
- No charting library: the skill's chart domain is for trend/comparison/proportion data visualization.
This dashboard has no charts -- it has a dependency graph (SVG connectors I own) and data tables. A
charting library would be a dependency with no job to do.
- TypeScript: the API surface (7 stages x 6 states, gate decisions, decision/ambiguity records) is exactly
the kind of shape that's easy to get subtly wrong at a fetch boundary. Typed responses catch that at
compile time instead of in a demo.
name: orchestration-dashboard
